title: Cerebral palsy and profound and multiple learning disabilities
blurb: Anticipate the health problems that come with cerebral palsy and PMLD, from aspiration and constipation to hip and spine pain, and coordinate complex care.
question: Nathan, 26, has cerebral palsy and profound and multiple learning disabilities and lives at home with his mother. For a week he has coughed during meals; today his temperature is 37.9 °C, his breathing is faster and he 'sounds chesty'. What should the community nurse do?

teach.h: A brain injury that does not progress
teach.body: Cerebral palsy is a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive disturbance of the developing brain. In plain English: an injury to the growing brain affects how the body moves, and that injury does not get worse. Many people with cerebral palsy do not have a learning disability; some have a learning disability, and some have profound and multiple learning disabilities (PMLD).

teach.h: The injury is fixed; the body changes
teach.body: The brain injury does not progress, but the body can change over time. Muscle tone and posture can lead to hip displacement, scoliosis and contractures, which cause pain and affect seating, breathing and swallowing. So a loss of function or new distress in someone with cerebral palsy is never 'just their CP': it needs assessment for a cause such as hip pain, infection or constipation.

teach.caption: Good positioning day and night reduces hip dislocation, scoliosis, chest infections and aspiration.

steps.label: Risk factors
steps.sub: Dysphagia, reflux, poor posture, epilepsy, poor oral health

steps.label: Aspiration
steps.sub: Food, fluid or saliva into the lungs

steps.label: Prevent
steps.sub: SLT plan, postural care, oral care, early treatment

teach.caption: People do not die 'of' cerebral palsy but of illnesses that follow, such as pneumonia.

teach.body: People with PMLD may see speech and language therapy, physiotherapy, dietetics, epilepsy and wheelchair services. Without coordination, families face conflicting advice. A named lead professional works with the family to bring plans together. Families and long-term carers know the person's baseline: how they show pain, pleasure and illness. Documenting this (for example with DisDAT) and listening to them is central to safe care.

Coughing at meals points to unsafe swallowing, and fever with faster breathing suggests a chest infection, possibly aspiration pneumonia. The nurse completes observations, sits Nathan upright and arranges same-day medical review rather than waiting. She asks for an urgent speech and language therapy review of his eating and drinking plan, checks oral care and his positioning, and records his mother's concern. Recognising pneumonia early is one of the clearest ways to prevent avoidable death.

teach.text: Three errors to avoid: 'his CP is getting worse' (the brain injury is non-progressive; look for a treatable cause), 'cerebral palsy means a learning disability' (often it does not), and writing 'cerebral palsy' as the cause of death instead of the illness that caused it.

items: Cerebral palsy: permanent movement and posture disorders, non-progressive brain injury; not always LD.
Look for epilepsy, dysphagia, reflux, constipation, chest infections, hip and spine pain.
24-hour postural care protects body shape and breathing.
Aspiration pneumonia: SLT plan, posture, oral care, early escalation.
PMLD: named lead professional; families' knowledge of the baseline.

summary: You can now explain what cerebral palsy and PMLD are, anticipate their linked health problems, and act early on signs of aspiration, constipation and musculoskeletal pain. You can also explain why postural care and coordinated, family-centred care save lives.

A.q: A healthcare assistant asks whether everyone with cerebral palsy has a learning disability. Which answer is accurate?
options: Yes, cerebral palsy is classed as a type of learning disability
Many people with cerebral palsy do not have a learning disability
A learning disability develops later as the brain injury progresses
The severity of movement problems shows the level of disability
A.why: Cerebral palsy is a disorder of movement and posture. Some people also have a learning disability, but many do not.

whyNot.0: Cerebral palsy is a movement disorder, not a type of learning disability.
whyNot.2: The brain injury in cerebral palsy is non-progressive.
whyNot.3: Physical severity does not predict intellectual ability.

A.q: Which statement best describes the main purpose of 24-hour postural care?
options: Building muscle strength so the person can walk
Keeping the person still to reduce their seizures
Protecting body shape and reducing hip and chest problems
Improving sleep by keeping one position all night
A.why: 24-hour postural care in lying, sitting and standing protects body shape and reduces hip dislocation, scoliosis, chest infections and aspiration.

whyNot.0: Postural care protects body shape; walking is not its main aim.
whyNot.3: Postural care uses supported positions; one fixed position all night can cause harm.

A.q: Kieran, 31, has cerebral palsy and PMLD. At lunch he coughs with each spoonful and his voice sounds wet. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give sips of water to help clear his throat
Continue slowly, as coughing clears the food
Switch to a softer food and finish the meal
Stop the meal, sit him upright and request SLT review
A.why: Coughing with each mouthful and a wet voice are signs of aspiration. Stop, position upright, observe and request speech and language therapy review.

whyNot.0: Thin fluids can be harder to swallow safely and may increase aspiration.
whyNot.1: Coughing shows food or fluid entering the airway; continuing risks pneumonia.
whyNot.2: Changing texture without assessment may not be safe and delays review.

B.q: Maya, 29, has cerebral palsy and PMLD and does not use words. She grimaces and arches her back when repositioned. Which approach to assessing her pain is most appropriate?
options: DisDAT, compared with her documented usual cues
A numerical rating scale from 0 to 10
A faces scale that she points to herself
Her heart rate within a NEWS2 assessment
B.why: DisDAT records a person's usual content and distress cues so changes can be recognised in someone who cannot report pain.

whyNot.1: Numerical scales need verbal understanding and expression.
whyNot.2: Pointing to a faces scale needs abilities Maya may not have.
whyNot.3: Heart rate is non-specific and misses her individual cues.

B.q: Which musculoskeletal problem is common in cerebral palsy and often causes pain on moving and difficulty with seating?
options: Gout
Rheumatoid arthritis
Carpal tunnel syndrome
Hip displacement
B.why: Hip displacement, with scoliosis and contractures, is common in cerebral palsy and causes pain and seating problems.

whyNot.0: Gout is not a typical complication of cerebral palsy.
whyNot.1: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease unrelated to cerebral palsy.
whyNot.2: Carpal tunnel syndrome is not a characteristic complication.

B.q: Lena, 33, has cerebral palsy and PMLD and takes two anti-seizure medicines. She has not had a bowel movement for four days, her abdomen is distended and she has vomited twice. What should the nurse do?
options: Give a laxative and check her bowel chart tomorrow
Escalate urgently for medical review today
Add extra fibre to her next feed and observe
Record it on her bowel chart and continue care
B.why: Distension and vomiting with no bowel movement suggest severe constipation or obstruction, which can be life-threatening. LeDeR shows constipation still contributes to deaths.

whyNot.0: Vomiting and distension need urgent medical assessment, not a wait.
whyNot.2: Extra fibre will not treat possible obstruction.
whyNot.3: Recording without escalating delays urgent assessment.

C.q: Nathan, 26, has cerebral palsy and PMLD. He has coughed during meals for a week. Today his temperature is 37.9 °C, his breathing is faster and his mother says he sounds chesty. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Thicken his drinks to level 4 and reassess in 48 hours
Encourage oral fluids and repeat observations tomorrow
Arrange same-day medical review for possible aspiration pneumonia
Lie him flat to rest and recheck his temperature later
C.why: Coughing at meals with fever and faster breathing suggests aspiration pneumonia, a leading cause of death in LeDeR. Same-day review, upright positioning and an urgent SLT review are needed.

whyNot.0: Changing texture without SLT assessment, and waiting 48 hours, delays treatment.
whyNot.1: Oral fluids may increase aspiration, and waiting a day is unsafe.
whyNot.3: Lying flat increases aspiration and reflux risk.

C.q: Reuben, 25, has PMLD and is admitted to hospital. His mother offers to stay overnight because she understands his signs of pain and distress. Ward visiting ends at 8pm. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Ask her to leave at 8pm in line with ward policy
Agree she can stay, as a reasonable adjustment
Let her stay if she gives his overnight personal care
Ask her to write his cues down and then go home
C.why: Flexible visiting so a carer who knows the person can stay is a reasonable adjustment under the Equality Act 2010 s20 and supports safe recognition of pain and deterioration.

whyNot.0: Applying the policy rigidly would put Reuben at a substantial disadvantage.
whyNot.2: The ward remains responsible for his care; her staying is not conditional on providing it.
whyNot.3: Written cues help, but her presence is a reasonable adjustment that supports his care.

C.q: Kieran, 31, has cerebral palsy and PMLD and has had three chest infections this year. Which plan best reduces his risk of aspiration pneumonia?
options: Thickened fluids for every drink, with no other changes
Antibiotics kept at home to start at the first cough
Meals given while he reclines, to slow his eating pace
An SLT eating plan with 24-hour postural and oral care
C.why: Prevention combines a speech and language therapy eating and drinking plan, 24-hour postural care, good oral care and early recognition of chest infection.

whyNot.0: Thickened fluids without assessment and wider measures is incomplete.
whyNot.1: Standby antibiotics do not prevent aspiration.

reteach.title: Fixed brain, changing body
reteach.question: If the brain injury in cerebral palsy does not get worse, why do problems keep appearing through life?

blocks.h: The body responds to tone and posture
blocks.body: Abnormal muscle tone pulls on bones and joints for years. Hips can slip, the spine can curve, the chest can become restricted and swallowing less safe. Each change brings pain and new risks. That is why posture, swallowing and pain are reviewed throughout life.

blocks.text: New distress on moving = look for pain (hips, constipation, reflux), not a behaviour plan.

explain.body: Permanent disorders of movement and posture from a non-progressive disturbance of the developing brain. A learning disability may or may not be present.

test.q: Which description of cerebral palsy is most accurate?
options: A slowly progressive disease of the nerves and muscles
Lasting movement and posture problems from early brain injury
A genetic syndrome caused by an extra copy of a chromosome
A form of learning disability with added physical needs
test.why: Cerebral palsy is a group of permanent movement and posture disorders from a non-progressive disturbance of the developing brain.

whyNot.2: Cerebral palsy is not a chromosomal syndrome.
whyNot.3: It is a movement disorder; a learning disability is not always present.

explain.body: Epilepsy, dysphagia, reflux, constipation, chest infections, pain, hip displacement and scoliosis. A loss of function needs assessment for a treatable cause.

test.q: Marta, 34, has cerebral palsy and a mild learning disability. Over a year she has needed more help to transfer from her wheelchair. She asks whether her cerebral palsy is getting worse. Which reply is most accurate?
options: Yes, cerebral palsy slowly worsens through adult life
No, so the change is most likely due to her age
The brain injury is fixed, but hips, spine and pain can worsen
Yes, so physiotherapy will no longer help her
test.why: The brain injury is non-progressive, but musculoskeletal problems, pain and fatigue can increase and need assessment.

whyNot.0: The brain injury itself does not progress.
whyNot.1: At 34, ageing is not a sufficient explanation; look for a cause.
whyNot.3: Physiotherapy and postural care remain important.

explain.body: Dysphagia, reflux, poor posture, epilepsy and poor oral health raise aspiration pneumonia risk. Prevention: SLT plan, 24-hour postural care, oral care and early treatment.

test.q: Owen, 15, has PMLD and is fed by gastrostomy. He arches his back and coughs when laid flat soon after feeds and has had two chest infections this term. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Reflux with risk of aspiration
Behaviour to avoid lying down
A dislocated hip on one side
Feed intolerance with diarrhoea
test.why: Distress and coughing when flat after feeds, with recurrent chest infections, suggest reflux with aspiration.

whyNot.1: Treating this as behaviour risks diagnostic overshadowing.
whyNot.2: Hip pain would not explain coughing and chest infections.
whyNot.3: Nothing in the history suggests diarrhoea.

explain.body: Many services, one person. A named lead professional coordinates with the family, whose knowledge of the person's baseline is essential.

test.q: Bea, 20, has PMLD. Her father, her main carer, says she has nine appointments a month with different services, and the advice often conflicts. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Reduce the number of services involved
Ask him to choose which advice to follow
Agree a named lead professional to coordinate care
Refer him to a carers' support group
test.why: A named lead professional integrates plans with the family and reduces duplication and conflict.

whyNot.0: Bea may need all these services; coordination is the issue.
whyNot.1: This leaves the burden of coordination with him.
whyNot.3: Carer support helps, but does not fix the coordination problem.
